subject: physics_2
question_text: Discuss the intensity of transmitted light when a Polaroid sheet is rotated between two crossed polaroids.

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: with I₀ the polarised intensity after P₁ and P₂ at angle θ to P₁, two applications of Malus law give I₃ = I₀ cos²θ cos²(90° − θ) = I₀ cos²θ sin²θ = (I₀/4) sin²2θ; maximum I₀/4 at θ = 45°, zero at θ = 0° and 90°; four maxima per full rotation. The book's printed algebra reaches the same result but writes it loosely (it mixes an unpolarised I/2 factor and two angles θ₁, θ₂ into what is a one-angle problem); the derivation here keeps the single angle θ and the clean I₀ throughout.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.
insider_note: The final form (I₀/4) sin²2θ and the θ = 45° maximum are what the examiner scans for — the two Malus-law applications are how you reach them.

steps.label: The three polaroids
steps.margin_note: No separate figure mark asked, but the picture fixes the set-up: P₁ axis vertical, P₃ axis horizontal (crossed), P₂ between them at angle θ. The dashed line in each sheet is its transmission axis.
steps.why: The whole problem is three transmission axes at three angles, and the picture is the fastest way to state them: vertical, θ, horizontal. Every cosine in the algebra is an angle between two of these dashed lines.
common_mistakes: Drawing P₁ and P₃ with parallel axes. Crossed means their axes are perpendicular.

recall.must_convey: That light passes through three polaroids in a row — P₁ and P₃ crossed, P₂ between them with its axis at θ to P₁.

steps.memory_tip: Three dashed axes: upright, tilted by θ, flat — the tilted one is the sheet that rotates.

steps.label: The arrangement
steps.mark_note: Crossed pair, θ defined, I₀ named
lines: P₁ and P₃ are crossed: their transmission
axes are perpendicular, so alone they pass
no light. A polaroid P₂ is placed between
them with its axis at angle θ to the axis
Let I₀ be the intensity of the polarised
steps.margin_note: First mark. Three facts: the pair is crossed, θ is measured from the axis of P₁, and I₀ is the intensity after P₁.
steps.why: Without P₂ the crossed pair is dark — that is the surprise the question is built on: inserting a third polaroid lets light THROUGH. Defining θ and I₀ here is what makes the two Malus-law steps one line each.
common_mistakes: Taking I₀ as the unpolarised intensity before P₁. Here I₀ is the polarised intensity after P₁; the unpolarised input would contribute a separate factor of 1/2.
Measuring θ from the axis of P₃ but then using cos²θ for the P₁ to P₂ step. Fix θ from the axis of P₁ and keep it fixed.

recall.must_convey: That P₁ and P₃ are crossed, P₂ sits between them at angle θ to P₁, and I₀ is the polarised intensity after P₁.
accept: theta from the axis of P1
I nought after the first polaroid
reject: cos squared theta by Malus law

steps.memory_tip: Crossed pair alone: dark. The question is what the middle sheet changes.

steps.label: Intensity after P₂ — Malus law
lines: By Malus law, the intensity transmitted
steps.margin_note: Second mark. One clean application of Malus law with the angle θ between the axes of P₁ and P₂.
steps.why: The light reaching P₂ is plane polarised along the axis of P₁, so Malus law applies directly with the angle between the two axes, θ. P₂ also turns the plane of polarisation to its own axis — which is what sets up the next step.
common_mistakes: Halving the intensity here. The light arriving at P₂ is already polarised; the factor 1/2 belongs only to unpolarised light.

recall.must_convey: That Malus law at P₂ gives I₂ = I₀ cos²θ.

steps.memory_tip: After P₂ the light is polarised along P₂'s own axis — remember that for the next step.

steps.label: Intensity after P₃
lines: The axis of P₃ makes (90° − θ) with the
axis of P₂. Applying Malus law again:
Using 2 sin θ cos θ = sin 2θ:
steps.margin_note: Third mark. The angle for the second application is (90° − θ), because P₁ and P₃ are crossed. Then the double-angle identity.
steps.why: P₁ to P₂ is θ and P₁ to P₃ is 90°, so P₂ to P₃ must be 90° − θ — the crossed condition is what fixes this angle. cos(90° − θ) = sin θ, and the double-angle identity packs cos²θ sin²θ into the single readable form (I₀/4) sin²2θ.
common_mistakes: Using θ again at P₃. The second Malus angle is between the axes of P₂ and P₃, which is 90° − θ.
Losing the factor 1/4: sin²θ cos²θ = (1/4) sin²2θ, since sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ.

recall.must_convey: That the P₂ to P₃ angle is 90° − θ, so I₃ = I₀ cos²θ sin²θ = (I₀/4) sin²2θ.
accept: cos squared theta sin squared theta
I nought by four sin squared two theta

steps.memory_tip: The three axes: 0, θ, 90°. The two gaps are θ and 90° − θ — one cosine each.

steps.label: The maximum
lines: I₃ is maximum when sin²2θ = 1, that is
I₃ is zero when θ = 0° or θ = 90° — the
crossed pair passes no light again.
As P₂ rotates through 360°, the light goes
steps.margin_note: Fourth mark. The discussion: maximum I₀/4 at 45°, zero at 0° and 90°, four maxima in one full rotation.
steps.why: The question says discuss, so the formula must be read out: sin²2θ peaks at 2θ = 90°, and because sin²2θ repeats every 90° of θ, one full turn of P₂ gives four maxima (45°, 135°, 225°, 315°) and four zeros.
common_mistakes: Giving the maximum as I₀. The best the arrangement passes is I₀/4, at θ = 45°.
Saying the light is brightest when P₂ lines up with P₁ or with P₃. At those settings (θ = 0° or 90°) the output is ZERO.

recall.must_convey: That the transmitted intensity peaks at I₀/4 when θ = 45°, is zero at 0° and 90°, and shows four maxima per rotation.

steps.memory_tip: Halfway between the crossed axes — 45° — is where the light gets through best.
